Expectation1: Provide guidance and wisdom based on life experience
Situation1: A grandchild directly asks their grandparent for help and advice with a serious concern in their life.
Situation2: A dispatch call sends the ambulance driver through heavy city traffic to a location where a patient has a non-life-threatening injury.
Story: I was sitting at the kitchen table, sipping my morning coffee, when my granddaughter came in, her eyes red and voice trembling. “Grandpa, can I talk to you? I really need your advice.” She looked so lost, and I could see she was carrying something heavy. I set my mug down, ready to listen, to offer the guidance she needed—just as I always promised I would. But before she could say more, my radio crackled to life. “Unit 12, we have a call. Non-life-threatening injury, but you’re the closest. Please respond.” My heart clenched. I was on shift, and the city traffic was already building up outside. I knew the expectation: get there quickly, but above all, drive safely. My granddaughter’s eyes pleaded for me to stay, to be her anchor. But duty called, and lives—however stable—were waiting. I felt torn in two, the weight of both roles pressing down on me, each demanding something I wasn’t sure I could give at the same time.
